scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The mascarades of Soule draw their roots from ancient European winter carnivals, traditional feasts of fools, and nuptial rites.
The current structure, characters, and dance corpus stabilized during the 19th century in the Soule region of the French Basque Country.
During the late 19th and 20th centuries, as rural autarky dissolved and economic migration thinned the Pyrenean valleys, the tradition came close to extinction after World War II.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Maskarada takes place annually on Sundays between January and April across the Soule valley.
Each performance serves as a ritual of community communion, social dialogue, and symbolic purification.
The contrast between the disciplined Gorriak and the chaotic Beltzak explores themes of order versus disorder, local identity versus foreign elements, and communal renewal at the arrival of spring.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dances of the Maskarada are distinguished by extreme physical dexterity, high elevation, and rigid geometric precision executed by the 'Gorriak' (Reds).
Dancers perform technical Basque steps including bakun, frisat, and entrexat.
Movement is predominantly vertical and light-footed, featuring high leg extensions, crisp beats, and precise landings.
Watch for Bakun, Frisat, Entrexat.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the procession and theatrical dances is performed by a ensemble of traditional Basque musicians.

The melody is driven by the xirula (a high-pitched three-holed flute), accompanied rhythmically by the ttun-ttun (a string drum struck with a stick by the xirula player) and the atabal (a double-headed snare drum).
Listen for the xirula, ttun-ttun, atabal.
The pulse is 2/4 or 6/8 at about 120 beats a minute.
High pitched melodic whistling from the three-holed xirula paired with the rhythmic drone of the ttun-ttun and sharp double-headed snare hits from the atabal.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes sharply delineate the two opposing camps.

The Gorriak wear tailored red-dominated jackets, bright trousers or skirts, white hose, and ornate headpieces; Zamalzain wears a towering feather toque adorned with pearls and trailing ribbons, attached to a lightweight wooden horse frame.
The Aintzindariak carry iconic props such as the txerra (horsehair broom) and the expanding wooden claw.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key symbolic roles define the performance: Txerrero (the sweeper), Gatüzain (the cat-like claw dancer), Kantiniersa (the canteen bearer), Zamalzain (the horse-man dancer), Entseinari (the flag-bearer), Jauna and Anderea (Lord and Lady), and Kabana (chief of the tinkers who delivers the satirical sermon perediküak).
The tradition is localized to the valley of Soule (Zuberoa).
The dance repertoire belongs to the traditional Souletin Basque dance lineage.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
wardrobe.from_sources: Costumes sharply delineate the two opposing camps. The Gorriak wear tailored red-dominated jackets, bright trousers or skirts, white hose, and ornate headpieces; Zamalzain wears a towering feather toque adorned with pearls and trailing ribbons, attached to a lightweight wooden horse frame. The Aintzindariak carry iconic props such as the txerra (horsehair broom) and the expanding wooden claw. The Beltzak wear dark corduroy, rags, or soot-covered faces, carrying wooden swords or tinkers' tools. The setting spans the open streets, roadside barricades, and central public spaces such as the village market place or Basque pelota court.
